title: Colombo Port: A Chinese exit gives Australia a renewed chance
author: Kulani Wijayabahu
text: |Sri Lanka, explained.Colombo, Sri Lanka (Thilina Alagiyawanna/Unsplash)Colombo Port: A Chinese exit gives Australia a renewed chanceAustralia’s lasting advantage in the Indian Ocean will come from building institutions, not simply replacing investors.Kulani Wijayabahu29 October 20264 min read|Colombo Port: A Chinese exit gives Australia a renewed chanceColombo Port: A Chinese exit gives Australia a renewed chanceChina’s withdrawal from a major logistics project at Sri Lanka’s Colombo Port this month presents Australia with an opportunity beyond replacing a Chinese investor. It raises a larger question: who will help smaller Indian Ocean countries develop the institutions needed to manage their ports, protect their waters and negotiate international investments?In October 2026, the Sri Lanka Ports Authority confirmed the termination of a Chinese-backed logistics venture (Opens in new window) established in 2023. Sri Lanka now intends to seek alternative investors through competitive bidding.Australia is well positioned to coordinate such an effort.Australia should take a leadership role not as a short-term response to China but as a long-term investment in its own security and prosperity.China’s wider maritime presence in Sri Lanka remains substantial. The cancellation does not signal Beijing’s departure. But it offers Canberra an opportunity to demonstrate what a different approach to regional cooperation could achieve.Australia has experience helping smaller countries strengthen maritime institutions.Building modern ports without investing in the institutions responsible for maritime safety leaves serious risks unresolved.In Sri Lanka, Australia has supported the installation of vessel-tracking equipment on more than 4,200 fishing vessels, alongside a monitoring centre. It has also provided maritime surveillance and hydrographic equipment.These initiatives demonstrate how Australian assistance can build a country’s ability to monitor its waters and manage maritime activities.The opportunity now is to turn individual projects into a sustained regional strategy.The Indian Ocean connects Australia to major markets across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Europe. Secure shipping routes depend not only on powerful navies but also on coastal countries having effective institutions, equipment and trained personnel.Sri Lanka’s own experience illustrates the stakes.X-Press Pearl, a container ship operated by Singapore based X-Press Feeders caught fire near Colombo Port in May 2021 (Nilantha Ilangamuwa/Unsplash)In May 2021, the X-Press Pearl container ship caught fire near Colombo and subsequently sank, triggering one of the country’s worst maritime environmental disasters.Plastic pellets, chemicals and other pollutants affected coastal communities and fishing livelihoods.The United Nations Environment Program’s assessment (Opens in new window) set out the scale and complexity of the disaster, including the risk of pollution spreading beyond Sri Lanka’s waters.Although Sri Lankan and Indian authorities responded to the emergency, the incident demonstrated why maritime countries need strong emergency-response systems, environmental regulators and the technical capacity to manage major shipping accidents.For Australia, the lesson is straightforward: building modern ports without investing in the institutions responsible for maritime safety leaves serious risks unresolved. Supporting them is a long-term investment in a safer and more resilient Indian Ocean.Australia’s first priority should be helping Sri Lanka strengthen the institutions responsible for managing its maritime economy. Ports require more than construction. They need transparent contracts, capable regulators, skilled professionals and financially sustainable management.Australian expertise in maritime safety, port administration, environmental protection and infrastructure governance could strengthen these foundations. There is already a practical model. The Australian Maritime Safety Authority’s regional cooperation programmes (Opens in new window) help neighbouring countries improve maritime safety, search-and-rescue capabilities and responses to marine pollution.Australia could expand this experience across the Indian Ocean, beginning with Sri Lanka.Canberra could also use the Quad Ports of the Future Partnership (Opens in new window) to coordinate investment expertise with India, Japan and the United States.India brings geographical proximity, Japan offers infrastructure know-how, and the United States could help mobilise financing. Australia could coordinate these strengths while supporting transparent investment arrangements and local expertise.This would demonstrate to Washington that effective regional leadership requires more than countering China’s influence. It requires building partnerships that deliver lasting economic and security benefits.Without sustained cooperation, smaller maritime countries may continue to face gaps in surveillance, technical expertise and infrastructure governance.These weaknesses can make it harder to prevent maritime accidents, combat illegal fishing and negotiate sustainable infrastructure agreements.They can also increase dependence on whichever external partner offers immediate financial or technical assistance.The concern is not simply which major power gains influence. It is whether smaller countries develop the ability to manage their own maritime futures.Australia cannot guarantee regional stability. But it can help reduce risks by strengthening the countries whose ports and waters support international trade.Sri Lanka should not be expected to choose between China and Australia. Maintaining relationships with multiple partners allows smaller countries to pursue investment opportunities while protecting their national interests.Australia’s contribution should be to expand those choices, not restrict them.Its existing development partnership with Sri Lanka (Opens in new window) provides a foundation for this approach.China’s Colombo Port withdrawal may have created the immediate opening, but Australia’s response should outlast this particular project.A secure Indian Ocean cannot be built by Australia alone. It requires capable maritime partners. Helping smaller countries become stronger is therefore not simply good regional diplomacy; it is an investment in Australia’s own future.About the authorKulani WijayabahuDr Kulani Wijayabahu is a former Senior Lecturer in the Department of International Relations at the University of Colombo, Sri Lanka, with more than a decade of experience in university-level teaching and research in International Relations.TopicsSri LankaTrade & investmentQuadChinaThe Interpreter on Sri LankaExplore The InterpreterIndiaCanberra should keep a close watch on the Colombo Security Conclave26 May 2026Lisa Singh,Tushar JoshiSri LankaAustralia should see Sri Lanka as more than a China–India contest14 May 2026Kulani WijayabahuBangladeshThe outside-in story that helps explain turmoil in Nepal, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka23 September 2025Nilanthi SamaranayakeMore on Sri LankaExplore Sri LankaEvent HighlightsSri Lanka’s debt crisis: preconditions, progress and politicsMariza Cooray, Roland Rajah
